documents.title: How can AI influence the economy and monetary policy?
documents.dateNote: “DATE: 19 May 2026” on the speech PDF. No views disclaimer was found in the PDF.

records.statement: In a speech of 25 January 2017, Mark Carney, Governor of the Bank of England and Chair of the Financial Stability Board, said that robo-advice and risk management algorithms in wholesale banking and markets may lead to excess volatility or pro-cyclicality through herding, particularly if the algorithms are highly correlated.
records.missing: The passage concerns algorithms and robo-advice generally; it does not attribute the herding risk to AI or machine-learning models, data or techniques.
records.qualification: The passage speaks of algorithms in general, within a speech on fintech; it does not name AI or machine learning as the source of the correlation. The speech elsewhere lists “innovations in machine learning” among enabling technologies. A statement of a possible risk, not evidence that it has materialised.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 11), section on systemic risks of fintech
evidence.passage: In wholesale banking and markets, robo-advice and risk management algorithms may lead to excess volatility or increase pro-cyclicality as a result of herding, particularly if the underlying algorithms are overly sensitive to price movements or highly correlated.

records.statement: The Bank of England (including the PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority state in Discussion Paper DP5/22 of 11 October 2022 that AI models may become correlated in subtle ways and add to risks of herding or procyclical behaviour in market stress, and that uniformity across firms’ models could amplify procyclical behaviour.
records.qualification: A discussion paper inviting responses; it states possible risks and does not record that herding from AI has occurred or adopt a policy.

evidence.passage: models may become correlated in subtle ways and add to risks of herding, or procyclical behaviour at times of market stress.
algorithms may result in uniformity across models and approaches at multiple firms, which could amplify procyclical behaviour and lead to herding in certain use cases, such as algorithmic trading.

records.statement: A special feature of the ECB’s Financial Stability Review of May 2024, prepared by Georg Leitner, Jaspal Singh, Anton van der Kraaij and Balázs Zsámboki, states that widespread AI adoption may harbour the potential for increased herding behaviour and market correlation, and that AI could lead to distorted asset prices, increased correlation, herding or bubbles.
records.qualification: A staff-prepared special feature published in the Financial Stability Review; the page carries no statement that it is the Governing Council’s view. It describes channels and conditions (technological penetration and supplier concentration), not observed herding.

evidence.passage: widespread AI adoption may harbour the potential for increased herding behaviour and market correlation.
As a result, AI may make market participants’ conclusions systematically biased, leading to distorted asset prices, increased correlation, herding behaviour or bubbles.

records.statement: The Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee states in its Financial Stability in Focus of 9 April 2025 that the potential for AI-based market participants to take increasingly correlated positions, driven by widespread use of a few models or data sets, is an important consideration from a systemic risk perspective and could amplify shocks in stress.
records.qualification: The text states that the practical implications are uncertain and that herding risks are not new and are already part of the FPC’s monitoring; it records a judgement of potential risk, not observed AI-driven herding.

evidence.locator: Section “Greater use of AI in financial markets”
evidence.passage: From a systemic risk perspective, the potential for AI-based participants to take increasingly correlated positions is an important consideration. This could be driven by the widespread use of a small number of open-source or vendor-provided models or underlying data sets

the potential future use of more advanced AI-based trading strategies could lead to firms taking increasingly correlated positions and acting in a similar way during a stress, thereby amplifying shocks.

records.statement: In a speech published on 30 June 2026, Sarah Breeden, Deputy Governor for Financial Stability at the Bank of England, said that AI agents responding similarly to the same prompts or triggers could amplify volatility in stress, and that the Bank is experimenting with simulation methods on which aspects of agent design could drive herding.
records.qualification: The speech states that trading firms for now mostly use autonomous AI for lower-risk tasks; the passage is about a possible future channel. No views disclaimer was found on the page; the speech is attributed to the speaker, not to the Bank.

evidence.passage: If AI agents respond similarly to the same prompts or triggers, they could amplify volatility in stress – especially if their objectives drift from original goals or public policy objectives
We are experimenting with the BIS Innovation Hub and the Bundesbank on simulation methods to understand which aspects of agent design could drive herding behaviour.

records.statement: The Bank of England (including the PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority state in DP5/22 of 11 October 2022 that increased reliance on third parties for datasets, AI algorithms and cloud computing may amplify systemic risks, as failures or cyberattacks at critical third parties could create a single point of failure affecting multiple firms and markets.
records.qualification: A discussion paper; it states a possible channel of systemic risk and refers to the separate DP3/22 on critical third parties. Not evidence that such a failure has occurred.

evidence.passage: operational failures and cyberattacks at critical third parties could result in disruption to certain AI services and therefore lead to a single point of failure that could impact multiple firms and markets.

records.statement: The ECB Financial Stability Review special feature of May 2024, prepared by Georg Leitner, Jaspal Singh, Anton van der Kraaij and Balázs Zsámboki, states that if most financial institutions use the same or very similar foundation models from a few suppliers, reliance on those providers increases and single-point-of-failure risks arise.
records.qualification: States a conditional channel (“supplier concentration”) and notes that future levels of concentration are difficult to predict; it cites concentration of investment in AI firms, not observed failures.

evidence.passage: If a majority of financial institutions use the same or very similar foundation models provided by a few suppliers, it is likely that decisions based on AI will suffer from similar biases and technological challenges, and reliance on system providers will increase.

Both would be amplified if the number of AI suppliers is limited, as this would additionally increase the financial system’s dependency on third-party providers and introduce single-point-of-failure risks.

records.statement: The Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee states in its Financial Stability in Focus of 9 April 2025 that reliance on a small number of providers for a given service could lead to systemic risks if they are disrupted, and that growing concentration in the supply of AI-related services could increase risks to the financial system.
records.qualification: The text also names factors that could reduce concentration, such as open-source models; it records a potential risk, not a disruption that has occurred.

evidence.locator: Executive summary, “Operational risks in relation to AI service providers”
evidence.passage: Reliance on a small number of providers for a given service could lead to systemic risks in the event of disruptions to them, especially if is not feasible to migrate rapidly to alternative providers.

evidence.locator: Section “Operational risks in relation to AI service providers”
evidence.passage: Growing concentration in the supply of AI-related services could increase risks to the financial system.

records.statement: In a keynote speech of 24 February 2026, Pedro Machado, ECB representative to the Supervisory Board, said that generative AI systems are often sourced from a small number of major third-party providers and that this raises supervisory concerns about concentration risk, vendor lock-in, operational resilience and exit strategies.
records.missing: The speech states that generative AI is sourced from a few major providers and that this raises supervisory concerns about concentration risk for banks; it does not state that many firms’ common dependence could make one provider’s failure or disruption affect many firms at once, or the financial system.
records.qualification: The speech addresses risks to individual banks from a supervisory perspective; its one mention of systemic scale concerns AI usage, not provider dependence. Recorded as context after the cross-family check (B71); it does not quantify concentration or state that a provider failure has occurred. No views disclaimer was found on the page.

evidence.locator: Section on generative AI, paragraph beginning “While many of these issues”
evidence.passage: generative AI systems are often sourced from a small number of major third-party providers and are heavily reliant on cloud infrastructure

From a supervisory perspective, this raises several concerns regarding concentration risk, vendor lock-in, data confidentiality and security, operational resilience and exit strategies, as well as legal and reputational risks.

crossFamily.result: corrected: articulates to bears on (context), as the checker found; quotations agreed. Former id am-u02-ssm-2026-machado-ai-governance.

records.statement: In opening remarks on 5 November 2025, Tuomas Välimäki, Member of the Board of the Bank of Finland, said that dependence on third-party service providers is a key concern and that authorities must identify the critical service providers behind banking services, including providers of AI models.
records.qualification: A short passage in opening remarks to a seminar; it names the dependency as a concern without assessing its size. No views disclaimer was found on the page.

evidence.passage: Cybersecurity risks and dependence on third-party service providers are also key concerns. It’s not enough to know which banks are systemically important. We must also identify the critical service providers behind our banking sector services, including the providers of AI models.

records.statement: The ECB Financial Stability Review special feature of May 2024, prepared by Georg Leitner, Jaspal Singh, Anton van der Kraaij and Balázs Zsámboki, states that criminals could adapt AI for cyberattacks, market manipulation and deepfakes, and its Box A (prepared by Sándor Gardó and co-authors) states that AI tools will enhance the capabilities of threat actors, including through deepfakes in phishing.
records.qualification: The box also states that AI benefits cyber defence and that it is difficult to assess which side will gain; the text records a change in capabilities, not a measured rise in losses attributable to AI.

evidence.locator: Section “Benefits and risks of AI for financial institutions”
evidence.passage: criminals could fine-tune and spoil otherwise harmless AI for specific operations (e.g. cyberattacks, misinformation, market manipulation, use of deep fakes to undermine confidence in a financial institution, etc.), increasing their threat potential.

evidence.locator: Box A “The implications of artificial intelligence for cyber risk: a blessing and a curse”
evidence.passage: AI tools will enhance the capabilities of threat actors while also benefiting cybersecurity.

records.statement: In a keynote speech in Rome on 4 July 2024, Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, said that a risk stemming from AI is the degree to which it can be used to spread false information, facilitate fraud or launch cyberattacks, including deepfakes of policymakers in a crisis.
records.qualification: The speech also states that AI can help detect such attacks; it names a risk for central banks and the public, not a recorded incident. No views disclaimer was found on the page.

evidence.locator: Section “The limits of AI: putting the necessary safeguards in place”
evidence.passage: The second risk stemming from AI is the degree to which it can be used to spread false information and data, facilitate fraud or launch cyberattacks.
But it is quite another when a deepfake of a policymaker goes viral – particularly at moments of crisis

records.statement: In a Euro & talous analysis of 5 September 2024 published by the Bank of Finland, economist Tatu Räsänen writes (in Finnish) that the spread of generative AI has already increased risks linked to cyber threats, information operations and fraud, that deepfakes make fraud easier, and that generative AI enables more sophisticated cyberattacks.
records.qualification: Quoted in the original Finnish; English paraphrase in the evidence notes. The article cites a US Treasury report for these points and carries a disclaimer that the views are the author’s. It states risk channels, not measured losses.

evidence.locator: Section “Generatiivisen tekoälyn yleistyminen voi lisätä epävakauttaviin kehityskulkuihin liittyviä riskejä rahoitussektorilla”, first paragraph
evidence.passage: Generatiivisen tekoälyn yleistyminen on jo lisännyt kybermaailmaan, informaatiovaikuttamiseen ja huijauksiin liittyviä riskejä.
evidence.note: English paraphrase: the spread of generative AI has already increased risks related to the cyber domain, information operations and scams.

evidence.passage: Huijauksista ja disinformaation levittämisestä on tullut yhä helpompia toteuttaa edistyksellisten syväväärennösten (deepfake) avulla. Tämän ohella generatiivinen tekoäly mahdollistaa sofistikoituneempien kyberhyökkäysten toteuttamisen.
evidence.note: English paraphrase: scams and the spreading of disinformation have become ever easier to carry out with advanced deepfakes; in addition, generative AI enables more sophisticated cyberattacks.

records.statement: In his Mansion House speech published on 14 July 2026, Andrew Bailey, Governor of the Bank of England, said that frontier AI’s ability to find and potentially exploit vulnerabilities in systems represents a major threat to the security of systems and so to financial stability, calling for coordinated testing of frontier models and stronger recovery capabilities.
records.qualification: The speech states the threat and policy responses; it does not report an incident. No views disclaimer was found on the page.

evidence.locator: Section on frontier AI, paragraph beginning “Let me turn to another aspect of AI”
evidence.passage: Suffice to say, it appears to have moved on very rapidly, and represents a major threat to the security of systems and thus in our world to financial stability.
the ability of cutting-edge models to find, and potentially to exploit, vulnerabilities in systems poses some very important public policy and regulatory challenges

records.statement: The Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority report “Machine learning in UK financial services” of October 2019 states that machine-learning models are often very large, non-linear and non-parametric, which makes them harder to understand and validate, so that certain forms of risk-taking could go undetected.
records.qualification: The passage is in a box on supervision and governance in the authorities’ own voice; elsewhere the report relays firms’ views that lack of explainability is a risk. It does not state that undetected risk-taking has occurred.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 14 (printed p. 14), Box 3 “Algorithm complexity, supervision and governance”
evidence.passage: ML models are often very large, non-linear and non-parametric. This makes it harder to comprehensively understand their properties and to validate them. This means certain forms of risk-taking could go undetected.

records.statement: The Bank of England (including the PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority state in DP5/22 of 11 October 2022 that the growing complexity of AI models can lead to a lack of explainability or interpretability (the “black box problem”) and that this can lead to prudential risks and may require extra care to ensure accountability and oversight.
records.qualification: A discussion paper; it describes risks and does not set new requirements.

evidence.passage: the complexity of AI models is increasing, which can lead to a lack of explainability or interpretability (known as the ‘black box problem’).
a lack of explainability or transparency in some AI models may mean extra care or actions are needed to ensure full accountability and sufficient oversight.

records.statement: In a keynote speech of 24 February 2026, Pedro Machado, ECB representative to the Supervisory Board, said that if a bank cannot explain why an AI model behaves as it does in terms meaningful for decision-making, it cannot truly control that model.
records.qualification: States a supervisory expectation in a speech; it does not report a specific bank’s failure. No views disclaimer was found on the page.

evidence.passage: If a bank cannot explain why an AI model behaves the way it does, in terms that are meaningful for decision-making, then it cannot truly control that model.

records.statement: In Bank of England Staff Working Paper No. 674 of September 2017, Chiranjit Chakraborty and Andreas Joseph introduce machine learning for central banking and policy analysis, present a case study projecting UK CPI inflation, and write that machine-learning models generally outperform traditional approaches in prediction tasks.
records.qualification: A staff working paper with the authors’ disclaimer; the authors also state that open questions remain about causal inference. Their result is from their own case studies, not an adopted forecasting practice.

evidence.passage: We introduce machine learning in the context of central banking and policy analyses.
Machine learning models generally outperform traditional modelling approaches in prediction tasks, while open research questions remain with regard to their causal inference properties.

crossFamily.result: earliest-located role moved to ECB Working Paper No. 352, April 2004 (am-u05-ecb-wp-352), found in the pass before 2016; recorded as a correction. The CNB paper of 2005 stays a lead (decision 16a).

records.statement: In a keynote speech in Rome on 4 July 2024, Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, said that AI enables real-time analysis of economic indicators and that ECB staff use AI to nowcast inflation, including web-scraped price data and large language models for data classification.
records.qualification: Describes uses by ECB staff as stated in a speech; it does not report an evaluation of forecast accuracy beyond the statement that the models perform well compared with conventional measures.

evidence.passage: AI also enables the real-time analysis of economic indicators, helping central banks to make more timely policy decisions
ECB staff use AI to nowcast inflation. This includes web-scraping price data and using LLMs for data classification.

records.statement: In opening remarks on 5 November 2025, Tuomas Välimäki, Member of the Board of the Bank of Finland, said that the Bank’s machine-learning “robot economist” forecasts Finnish GDP growth with the latest data in a nowcasting model, and that central banks’ typical machine-learning uses include GDP nowcasting and crisis prediction.

records.statement: In a keynote speech of 23 March 2026, Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, said that the ECB has expanded AI and machine-learning tools aimed at forecasting, alternative data and nowcasting, including quantile regression forests for density forecasts of inflation used in forecasting exercises.

records.statement: In the Whitaker Lecture of 14 September 2018, Mark Carney, Governor of the Bank of England, said that “the appropriate setting of monetary policy will be influenced by” the structural changes of a Fourth Industrial Revolution, which he described as driven by advances in AI, automation and interconnectedness, including through the labour market, price dynamics and the equilibrium rate of interest.
records.qualification: The speech speaks of a “Fourth Industrial Revolution” of which AI is one named component, not of AI alone. It states an expected influence on policy, not a policy decision.

evidence.passage: The appropriate setting of monetary policy will be influenced by the structural changes wrought by the Fourth Industrial Revolution, including in the labour market, by its impact on price dynamics and on the equilibrium rate of interest.

records.statement: In a keynote speech in Rome on 4 July 2024, Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, said that AI could affect the economy in areas particularly relevant for monetary policy, including prices, monetary policy transmission and the natural rate of interest, which could move up or down depending on AI’s effects.

If AI boosts productivity growth and potential output, we may see upward pressure being exerted on the natural rate of interest, as demand increases for capital to invest in new technologies and expand production capabilities.

records.statement: The Bank of England states in its report of 15 October 2025 on its approach to innovation in AI, distributed ledger technology and quantum computing that technological innovation can affect potential output, labour market slack and household behaviour, that these effects are relevant for monetary policy decisions and transmission, and that agentic AI could affect inflation dynamics and measurement.
records.qualification: The passage speaks of technological innovation in general, with agentic AI named; it is a general statement of relevance, not an assessment of the size of AI’s effects.

evidence.passage: These effects are relevant for monetary policy decisions and may also affect monetary policy transmission.

records.statement: In a keynote speech of 23 March 2026, Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, set out how AI could affect inflation, the natural rate of interest (R*) and cyclical shocks, said that the net effect on R* remains uncertain, and said that the short- and longer-run effects of AI warrant careful monitoring for monetary policy.
records.qualification: The speaker states that the views are his own and not the Governing Council’s. He also states that the latest staff estimates of R* show no material change; the speech does not announce a policy response.

evidence.locator: Section “Implications of AI for monetary policy”
evidence.passage: Given these different mechanisms, the net effect of the AI transition on R* remains uncertain.

records.statement: In a speech of 19 May 2026, Aino Bunge, First Deputy Governor of Sveriges Riksbank, said that AI can drive policy rates up or down through productivity, the neutral rate, investment demand and asset prices, and that while AI has not yet affected current monetary policy, the Riksbank will have to monitor developments.

records.statement: In Bank of England Staff Working Paper No. 674 of September 2017, Chiranjit Chakraborty and Andreas Joseph present a case study that models the detection of alerts on financial institutions’ balance sheets for banking supervision with machine-learning methods, which they write generally outperform traditional approaches in prediction.

records.statement: In a speech of 4 June 2019, James Proudman, Executive Director of UK Deposit Takers Supervision at the Bank of England, said that AI and machine learning are helping firms in anti-money laundering and fraud detection and that machine learning may also improve the quality of credit risk assessments.

records.statement: The Bank of England (including the PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority state in the foreword to DP5/22 of 11 October 2022 that, given the overlap of existing sectoral rules that apply to AI, their approach is largely limited to clarifying how the existing framework applies to AI and addressing identified gaps.

records.statement: In a speech of 19 May 2022, Joachim Wuermeling of the Deutsche Bundesbank said that the results of the Bundesbank–BaFin consultation make clear that machine learning does not need its own new set of rules, and that the current technology-neutral and risk-oriented approach should provide a general framework for it.

records.statement: The Bank of England (including the PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority report in feedback statement FS2/23 of 26 October 2023 that most respondents to DP5/22 favoured a technology-neutral approach and considered that many AI risks could be mitigated within existing frameworks.

records.statement: In a speech published on 31 October 2024, Sarah Breeden, Deputy Governor for Financial Stability at the Bank of England, said that a technology-agnostic approach has so far worked well for AI and machine learning and that the Bank is not yet at the point of needing to change its tech-agnostic microprudential approach, while regulators should keep assuring themselves it remains sufficient.

records.statement: In a speech published on 30 June 2026, Sarah Breeden, Deputy Governor for Financial Stability at the Bank of England, said that, as AI capabilities increase, “we must keep asking” whether existing, technology-agnostic regulatory frameworks remain sufficient, that they were not built to contemplate autonomous agents, and that more sophisticated governance and accountability frameworks may be needed.
records.missing: The speaker states that existing frameworks were not built to contemplate autonomous agents and that more sophisticated governance and accountability frameworks “may be needed”, framed as a question to keep asking about agents; she does not state that existing frameworks fail to cover AI broadly or that a separate AI framework is needed.
records.qualification: Re-read under decision 18a: a question and a possible adaptation for autonomous agents, not a contest of broad coverage. She does not propose specific AI-specific rules. Compare her speech of 31 October 2024 (am-u12-boe-2024-breeden-engaging-machine). The cross-family checker (second check, A2.8) reads the passage as a qualified, prospective contest of continuing sufficiency for autonomous agents (frameworks not built for them; a human in the loop unlikely to be realistic), while noting that the pack’s distinction is reasonable and that the next sentence allows adapted governance frameworks. The record keeps that uncertainty.

evidence.locator: Section “Agentic payments and commerce”, final paragraph
evidence.passage: as AI capabilities increase, we must keep asking whether existing, technology-agnostic regulatory frameworks remain sufficient. Our frameworks were not built to contemplate autonomous agents, and relying on a human in the loop for all agent actions is unlikely to be realistic.

crossFamily.result: re-read: contests to bears on (context). Former id am-u12-boe-2026-breeden-agents-of-change-contests. Second check (2026-11-04, A2.8): the checker’s blind answer is a qualified prospective contest; its comparison accepts the pack’s reading under decision 18a and asks that the uncertainty be kept, not that the classification be overridden. Kept as bears on, with the checker’s reading in the qualification; no earliest-located role or headline is affected.

omissions.item: Andrew Haldane, “Will Big Data Keep Its Promise?” (Bank of England, 19 April 2018)
omissions.reason: Read; describes machine learning used on Bank statistics and supervisory letters (U05, U09) but is later than SWP 674 on both; left out for size.

omissions.item: Christine Lagarde, “The transformative power of AI” (ECB, 1 April 2025)
omissions.reason: Read; on productivity, investment and labour, with no passage tying AI’s effects to monetary policy, so it does not meet U06.

omissions.item: Andrew Bailey, “Can AI make cutlery?” (Bank of England, 21 May 2026)
omissions.reason: Read; on AI as a general purpose technology and growth, without a monetary-policy passage.

omissions.item: Piero Cipollone, digital euro speeches of 24 March 2026 and 6 October 2026, and “The transformation of money” (8 December 2025)
omissions.reason: The 2026 speeches name AI in payments only as an area to investigate or explore (no statement that agents change payment flows); the 2025 speech has no AI passage.

omissions.item: FS2/23 relays of respondents’ views on herding and deepfakes (U01, U03)
omissions.reason: Relays of anonymised respondents only; recorded for U12 where the relay is central, not for U01 or U03.
States that supervisors neither require nor prohibit technologies, which does not state that existing frameworks broadly cover AI; Proudman’s speech holds the U12 articulation for 2019.

omissions.item: Bank of Finland blog “Tekoäly tukee keskuspankkien analyysityötä” (Joni Heikkinen, Euro & talous, 2025)
omissions.reason: Retrieved; on text analysis of ECB communication with AI models (U05). No publication date could be read from the retrieved page, so it was not recorded.

omissions.item: ECB FSR May 2024 sentence on the current regulatory framework (U12)
omissions.reason: States that targeted initiatives may be needed if concerns arise that the current framework cannot tackle; too conditional to record without stretching U12.

omissions.reason: Located by discovery search; Wuermeling’s speech reports the consultation results and is recorded instead. The papers were not retrieved for lack of time.
